s: A company has several AWS accounts. A development team is building an automation framework for cloud governance and remediation processes. The automation framework uses AWS Lambda functions in a centralized account. A solutions architect must implement a least privilege permissions policy that allows the Lambda functions to run in each of the company's AWS accounts. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
o: In the centralized account, create an IAM role that has the Lambda service as a trusted entity. Add an inline policy to assume the roles of the other AWS accounts.
In the other AWS accounts, create an IAM role that has minimal permissions. Add the centralized account's Lambda IAM role as a trusted entity.
In the centralized account, create an IAM role that has roles of the other accounts as trusted entities. Provide minimal permissions.
In the other AWS accounts, create an IAM role that has permissions to assume the role of the centralized account. Add the Lambda service as a trusted entity.
In the other AWS accounts, create an IAM role that has minimal permissions. Add the Lambda service as a trusted entity.

w.y: Cross-account access works by the caller assuming a role in the target account. The Lambda execution role in the central account trusts lambda.amazonaws.com and has permission to sts:AssumeRole into the other accounts, and each target account has a least-privilege role that trusts the central Lambda role.

o.A: Correct: the Lambda execution role (trusted by the Lambda service) is allowed to assume the target-account roles.
o.B: Correct: each target account's minimal-permission role trusts the central Lambda role.
o.C: Trust is reversed; the central role does not need to trust the other accounts' roles.
o.D: Target accounts do not need to assume the central role, and the Lambda service there is irrelevant.
o.E: Trusting the Lambda service in target accounts lets only local Lambda functions use the role, not the central account's functions.
